en: Preface to the *Chanlin Baoxun Niansong* (Verses on the Precious Admonitions of the Zen Forest):
If one’s learning does not investigate the admonitions, it will not be extensive; if one’s questioning does not examine the admonitions, it will not be thorough;

if one’s reflection does not verify the admonitions, it will not be prudent; if one’s discernment does not detail the admonitions, it will not be clear; and if one’s practice does not rely upon the admonitions, it will not be steadfast. Thus, that which is cherished as precious serves to transform the mundane.
This is the standard for attaining sagehood. The argument is that while laws establish the great principles, reason accords with human sentiment;

since this has always been a matter of open and unencumbered freedom, why must one be so constrained? *Ei!* Among all things in the world, nothing is more difficult to gather and manage than those with whom one shares the transmission of the Dharma.
Looking up, one sees no heaven; looking down, one sees no earth. Let them roam freely through mountains and rivers; they are utterly without [artifice].

To exercise self-restraint and discipline is truly the manner of one who transcends their lineage; yet when it comes to actual practice, they merely sink into the indulgence of desires and blend with the secular world like dust.
Instead, they falsely claim this as "saving sentient beings," boastfully exaggerate it as "propagating the ancestral Way," or even flaunt it as "widely cultivating conditions for enlightenment.
Although these words may momentarily deceive the ignorant by appealing to the literal texts, how could they ever restrain the wise?
Is this not a case of sheer collapse? Please observe those such as Cheng Ren and his ilk;

they are constantly on the road—through the three capitals and four Bian rivers—seeking someone who can follow ancient admonitions and accord with the ancient pivot to serve as a model for future generations. Yet such people are truly rare.

It is all because they are negligent toward actual study; they grasp at superficial similarities to indulge in idle discourse, fail to seek out instruction, and instead use a jumble of stale clichés to obscure the truth.

Concealing [one's faults], one contemplates income and expenditure morning and evening; yet regarding the affairs of birth and death, they have already passed by more than half. Upon encountering debate or difficulty, one immediately becomes angry;

being coarse and superficial, one deceives oneself. As for the refined details of practice, one does nothing but occupy the monastery and transcribe records of sermons, merely transmitting them to a few monastics.
Examining this closely, it is evident that the Chan school is daily declining and true faith is daily diminishing—all of which are but shadows and echoes.
This current state has come about through the accumulation of imitative practices and mutual negligence.

It is fitting that we rely upon the earnest instructions of the venerable masters of the past—such as Mingjiao, Song, Yuan, Tong, and Ne—to begin by eradicating evil habits and turning the mind toward goodness, thereby restoring the sublime models of conduct within this pure and auspicious era.
If there are those who possess outstanding talent and the discerning eye to perceive the hidden resolve of Huiyun in rejecting heterodoxy and returning to the orthodox, it would be well...
How vast and expansive is his capacity! How precise and discerning is his inner core! He dwells in tranquility through prudence, responding to phenomena with luminous clarity.

Is he not indeed one who is steadfast, profound, and honors ritual propriety? I have rashly attempted this compilation, scouring the various quarters for their ailments and infirmities to the point of exhausting my very sinews;
yet even in drafting these admonitions and inscriptions for the Venerable Master, I still feel constrained by limitations. Alas! When things are in such a state of flood...

In this autumn, malevolent spirits pervade the wilds. Were it not for a man of fierce and ardent resolve, who has made a great vow and wields majestic authority, standing firm and heroic beyond the realm of sound, color, wealth, and profit, and who strives with capability, courage, and decisive judgment, he would have failed to compile these works.

Thus, he has taken the virtuous words, teachings, and meaningful phrases of the forty-two venerable patriarchs recorded in the past, extracted their essentials, and composed verses upon them, revising and arranging seventy-four pieces in total.

To cause them to tread together and gaze at one another’s brows, so that they may discern good from evil—yet you hastily speak of "adding frost to snow. I fear deeply that you will freeze these young people to death! Ha ha!
Written in the spring of the Jiawu year by the thirty-second generation successor of the Linji Orthodox Lineage, the Abbot of Huiyun Temple.

*Chanlin Baoxun Niansong* (Verses on the Precious Instructions of the Chan Forest), composed by Xingsheng, the Elder "Bao."
Attendant Chao recorded this;
the disciples Zhang Wenjia and Gu Rujin collated it together. Mingjiao Song said:
"The learning of the sages and worthies is not accomplished in a single day. When the daylight is insufficient, one must continue by night."

Accumulated over months and years, it naturally becomes perfected. [The Master] remarked: "I have investigated this with diligence for over twenty years, so that I might attain a state of total emptiness. He then offered this verse:
Penetrating the profound and subtle, my thoughts rest here; As months pass and years renew, may you protect and sustain this through empowerment.
If one speaks of those with sincere resolve who burn oil by night to continue their studies, Only when they spread [the teachings] before others do the multitude begin to know them.
Yuantong Ne said: "Throughout my life, I have practiced the wisdom of knowing when to act and when to stop, never burdening myself with fame or profit. If I were weary..."
Regarding the mind: when will it ever be satisfied? [The Master] comments: "One who knows where to stop can naturally abide in their lot;
yet people are busily burdened by toil because they do not weary of their own minds. The verse says:
Banishing sound and form, one attains eternal joy; Flying freely like wild cranes soaring through the clouds, Even if caught by a flying net, they cannot be bound or tethered.
The blue sky stretches ten thousand miles, vast and empty. Yuantong said:
"A person beneath the forest trees has nothing to guard. Those who rely on external power to establish their importance will, in a single moment, lose it."
What one clings to cannot avoid the calamity of falling and drowning. [The Master] remarked: "One creates it oneself and must suffer it oneself; there is no way to save oneself. He further said:
"Those who tread upon the tracks of clinging to power would do well to change their course with all haste. The verse says:
Carefully observing what is appropriate for one’s station as a monk, yet rushing toward power and aligning with influence, one enters into emptiness and peril.
When such a person encounters calamity and misfortune, they resent their fate and blame others; their folly is even more foolish than folly itself.
Dajue Lian said: "If a person does not study, they will not know the Way. Those predecessors who established themselves and achieved renown in their time...
Rarely is one not perfected through study and inquiry. [The Master] remarked: "One's reputation and status depend upon being cultivated through study and inquiry;
yet there are also those who achieve renown without such study. I do not know what authority they have for this. He then offered this verse:
Occupying this seat as a master, one’s talent and wisdom must not be derived from mere shallow learning;

it is only by relying on those of long-standing virtue that the model for others can be established. Cleverness and artifice will ultimately lead to failure, as Qian Xuan said of Shun and Yuan Yun of Fushan:
"If one wishes to investigate the unsurpassed, wondrous Way, one must become even more firm when in distress; when old, one should [be steadfast]."
It becomes even more robust. One must not follow worldly customs; if one merely covets fame and profit, one will lose the ultimate virtue for oneself. He remarked:
"The cultivation of the Way and its Virtue is something difficult to discuss with the teachers of the current vulgar age. The verse says:
"Grind yourself to perfection and preserve your integrity; value diligent application. Abide securely in the principles of meaning and refine your learning and insight.
How could you be like those who steal reputations and practice deception, greedily pursuing petty gains amidst chaotic turmoil?
Master Yuan said to Daowu, "If your study has not yet reached the Way, yet you flaunt your learning and insight, racing about with intellectual cleverness."
Those who seek to prevail through the sharpness and eloquence of their speech are like a latrine house; though it be smeared with vermilion and lacquer, it only serves to increase its stench.
[The Master] remarked: "What use is there for these slick-lipped Chan practitioners? He then offered this verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions to provide only the translation.]
Vaguely heard from the roadside and repeated on the path, it is certainly not like ivory growing on a dog’s tongue;
let the ugly wife imitate the frown of others at her own peril, for the unattractive woman’s painted face only adds to her clumsiness.
Wuzu Yan said to Fojian: "The essentials of being a *zhuchi* (abbot) lie in appearing dignified and full when presiding over the assembly, while in one's personal conduct, one must strive for..."

Be frugal with what you possess. As for all other trivial matters, do not concern yourself with them at all. The Master remarked: "To diminish oneself and benefit the assembly is the constant duty of a monk;
those who harbor thoughts of surplus are surely vulgar and base. To call such people 'Abbot' is a source of shame—shame upon shame! He further said:
"Only one who looks after their own fundamental nature can truly be granted this. The verse says:
Upholding the precepts with dignity, one practices the Way of the Dharma; Whether the household is wealthy or frugal, all is done with a sincere heart.
How could one act with private greed for self-indulgence? For practical use, a broken-legged cauldron is sufficient.
The Fifth Patriarch said: "In the monasteries of today, those who study the Way do not have their reputations spread abroad, nor are they trusted by others."

This is because their holy life (*brahmacarya*) is not pure; they are not upright as persons, but instead recklessly and covetously seek fame, reputation, profit, and offerings, flaunting their outward adornments.
Consequently, they are censured by those who possess discernment. The commentary states:
"Those who do not act with integrity are solely preoccupied with making a living through fame and profit; they should be expelled. The verse says:
Defiled and mixed with swine and pigs, they utter empty words that merely mock and disregard their own entrails and bellies;
yet in this present life, they indulge in such foolishness and indulgence that they bring shame upon the very flesh and bones of Shaolin.
Baizhang Yuanwen said to Yang Cigong: "If something can be spoken but cannot be practiced, it is better not to speak it at all. If something can be practiced..."
It may be said: "If it is not as it should be, do not act upon it. One must deliberate on the ultimate consequence of every word spoken;
one must examine the potential obscurations of every action undertaken. The commentary states: "When speech and conduct are in accord, one may truly be called Samantabhadra-rāja. The verse says:
Deep in learning and vast in wisdom, his considerations for affairs are thorough; with each passing season of肃杀 (su shā), autumn arrives once more.
Serenely, there is no duality between the inner and the outer; leaning over the marketplace, he rolls the embroidered ball.
Baiyun said: "Is the flourishing or decline of the Way something fixed? It depends on the person to propagate it. Therefore, when one maintains it, it remains; when one abandons it, [it perishes]."

Gone. Yet it is not that the Way departs from people; rather, it is people who depart from the Way. [The Master] remarked: "When one encounters a person who has departed from the Way, decline is close at hand.
How can one not be cautious? The verse says:
The wise rise and the foolish fail; greatness still awaits those who are truly heroic and transcendent.
To reveal the subtle intent is like the brilliance of the sun; when the bright day shines, how can the deluded ghosts and monsters find a place?

Thus says the White Cloud. It is often seen that many monastics have never contemplated plans for the far-reaching and the great. I fear that, from within the monastic groves, [the tradition will decline].
This is a time of decline and thinning. My late master Yangqi used to say that "everyone seeking security for themselves, whether superior or inferior, is the greatest affliction of the Dharma-gate.
He added, "To seek security through negligence is to fail to contemplate the far-reaching and the great; the ruin of the Dharma-gate all begins here.
He further said, "When petty men usurp authority, what kind of order can there be? Is there not a sense of profound lamentation? The verse says:
When a heavy burden is entrusted, one must expect to travel far; with constant diligence and reverent trepidation, do not falter.
I respectfully consider that where the transformative power of virtue prevails, those who are biased and depraved are transformed—like a wild jackal being made to crouch as a lion.
Baiyun said: "Zen practitioners possess much insight regarding what has already occurred, yet they lack the ability to perceive what is yet to come. This is the essence of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Concentration and wisdom prevent [delusion] before it has arisen; activity, cessation, spontaneity, and extinction awaken one after it has already occurred. The Master remarked: "Those who can awaken to what has already occurred are few; how many more, then, can apply their attention before it has even arisen? He further said: "The study of concentration and wisdom is precisely the embankment against those who indulge in activity and cessation. "Pity those who abandon their path halfway; take them back to their native land and apply the whip with renewed vigor.
Only by reaching the highest peaks and the furthest distances will one finally arrive. What could prevent the Seven Buddhas from joining arm to shoulder?
Ying of Shaowu, whenever he saw those who were unrestrained and fearless of cause and effect, would sigh: "A weary life is like a traveler’s lodging; if one stays..."
It follows conditions; once it departs, it is gone. What could that which was attained possibly amount to? You lot do not recognize integrity or shame;

you violate the boundaries of proper relationship and defile the religious teachings to such an extent. [The Master] picked up his whisk and said: "Those who lack integrity and shame cannot endure the censure."
It is permissible to view this as the way of a common person. The verse says:
In the swift passage of time, one calculates for longevity; Amassing wealth, one purchases estates and occupies mountain fields.
Before life ends, all clever and ingenious schemes are exhausted; After death, there is strife and contention over the walls.

Ying Shaowu said: "A great man whose ambition lies in expanding the ancestral Way and guiding future generations ought not to privately indulge his own desires without restraint, thereby inviting calamity upon himself and creating disaster for ten thousand kalpas. The three paths and the hells are not yet the ultimate suffering;
to lose one's human form beneath the *kāṣāya* is truly the suffering. [The Master] picked up the staff and said: 'To pursue private desire...'"
To lose one's human body is not to be called a great man. To warn him, the verse says:
"The Master who examines the school must first rectify himself; When the form is upright, the shadow is straight—perfect and beautiful.
The nostrils of the Vast Sky support the forest of the assembly; Tigers roar and dragons cry, and wind and mist arise."
Ying Shaowu said to Huìtáng, "In the Dharma-ending age, bhikṣus do not cultivate morality or the Way; they often engage in bribery and are coarse and unrefined.
They wag their tails to beg for pity and pursue fame and profit at the gates of those in power. Once their karma is full and their merit exhausted, [they fall]."
The devas and humans grew weary of it. [Zhaozhou] picked up the case and said: "These are all of the same class as those who break into houses and dig through walls. He then offered this verse:
Forming worldly attachments and bestowing wide renown, Through entanglements one creates karma—whom does it concern?
When King Yama calculates the tally, the offense is hard to escape; One must go to repay the debt, wearing horns and clad in fur.
Zhenjing’s *Wen* says: "In the Dharma of the Final Age, bhikṣus rarely possess integrity and righteousness. Whenever they engage in lofty talk and grand discourse, no one can match them;
yet when it comes to the kindness of a single meal, they differ at the beginning and assist at the end, first disparaging and later praising.

To seek those who say 'right' is right and 'wrong' is wrong, being upright and impartial without concealment, is rare indeed. [The Master] added: "I have encountered slander because of my uprightness and impartiality."
This, however, is not a definitive judgment. Although this old monk has never passed such a verdict, it is truly lamentable. The verse says:
The living fish’s gills are caught by the hook; Who would have thought it would face the turbid stream or the clear current?
Surrendering its body and accepting its fate according to its allotment, It covers its eyes before the present and lets even its transgressions rest.
Zantang Zhun said to Miaoxi, "In this age of the Dharma’s semblance, bhikṣus mostly pursue external objects while failing to clarify their own minds within.

Even if they engage in great deeds of propagation, none of these reach the ultimate. This is because that which they rely upon is base and vulgar; it is for this reason that things turn out thus. [The Master] comments:
Everyone expounds the Dharma, yet each one clings to conditions. Is it the mind pursuing objects? Or is it objects pursuing the mind? Please discern this. The verse says:
Carrying sand with the intent to fill a bottomless pit— In vain one expends the efforts of spirits and ghosts to transport it.
The fundamental nature is inherently luminous, yet it is neglected; Following the waves and drifting with the current, how pitiable!
Zantang said: "The Way is the true authority of past and present. For those who skillfully propagate the Way, the essential lies in adaptability. If one does not know how to adapt..."
These individuals cling to the literal teachings and become mired in appearances and attachments; all of them fail to comprehend the skillful application of means (*upāya*). The commentary states:
"One who penetrates the universal way is able to exercise skillful means. If one attains this realization, is not the Way found right here? The verse says:

Transcending names and transcending forms, it is even more perfectly transformative; the ancestral intent and the Buddha-mind are strung together on a single thread, the sovereign handle firmly held within one’s hand.
To turn back decline and restore what has been ruined, one must admire those who are called virtuous.
Zhan Tang said to Miaoxi: "In practicing Chan, you must recognize that your discernment must be lofty and far-reaching, and your resolve and spirit must be transcendent. When you speak..."

In one's conduct, maintain integrity toward others; do not yield to power or profit through deceitful crookedness. Do not allow yourself to be shaped by your peers or swayed by the fluctuations of the times.
He remarked, "Such a person is rarely encountered. The verse says:
Magnanimous Chan master, whom the world could not bind; taking vast strides through the Great Dharma, he manifested an exemplary demeanor.
Though he was one who stood apart and transcended all, he grasped the authority of transformation and relied upon his stewardship.
Lingyuan Qingwei called him "Longling Zhuo," saying: "The time for the practice of the Way has come; Ciming let his mind roam freely throughout Jing and Chu, even while harboring a sense of shame."
He endured insults, and those who saw him treated him with contempt. Ming laughed and said, "A city of jewels colliding with rubble—I knew from the start it would not prevail.

When he finally beheld the divine cauldron, his reputation spread throughout the monastic community, and he ultimately gave rise to the Way of Linji. The Master commented: "Sunk in obscurity, he was utterly unrecognized;
yet sitting there, he cut off the paths of gods and men, and all admired him. The Verse says:
The treasure-trove of forbearance is not worth a penny; when the time comes to encounter rare jewels, it is spread far and wide.
I send these words to say: if one possesses musk, it naturally emits its fragrance;
why must one stand tall against the wind? Lingyuan said to Huang鲁直 (Huang Tingjian): "In my ordinary daily life and leisure, I rarely give thought to birth-and-death or calamity. One...

In the morning, he went out on an unpredictable errand; [the Master] was just then stamping his feet and wringing his hands, trying to rescue him, but in the end could not save him. [The Master] remarked:
"If a person lacks far-reaching foresight, they will surely have immediate anxieties. The verse says:
Silently operating profound mechanisms before omens appear, one may eliminate calamities and enjoy long-lasting years of peace.
Yet, arrogance, extravagance, debauchery, and dissipation bring about the seeds of disaster; to rely idly upon withered mulberry trees while weeping with flowing tears is in vain.
Master Lingyuan said to the Monk Gu: "Calamity and fortune lean upon each other; good and ill share the same domain. It is only man who summons them himself; how can there be peace?"
How can one not contemplate this? [The Master] picks up the theme, saying: "Therefore, the gentleman must be cautious when he is alone.
The verse says: "The three realms are created solely by the mind; Safety and peril, gain and loss, are all weighed upon the scale.
One should know that the turning of earth and the revolving of heaven Rely especially upon the Great Hero’s solemn covenant."
Lingyuan said to Cheng Yichuan, "Many hardships fulfill one's aspirations; an absence of hardship leads to the ruin of one's person.
Therefore, the gentleman remains calm yet does not forget danger; he maintains order yet does not forget chaos. [The Master] comments:

Only those who have been polished by trials and tribulations can truly grasp such words. He further says: This is also the essential secret for navigating the world and governing oneself. The verse says:
Walk with straightforwardness and always guard yourself in secret against stumbling; having traversed rugged paths, exert yourself and know that the Buddha refines one through demons.
"Copper Eyes and Iron Spine" shall forever protect the three thousand worlds. Lingyuan said:
Among those who have passed the station of abbotship, few are able to see it through to the end. This is because their merit and virtue are shallow, and their capacity...
To cross a narrow pass, one’s learning and insight are base and shallow; yet being unable to follow what is good and strive for righteousness to broaden oneself, such a state results.
The Master remarked: "This is precisely what is meant by a small boat being unable to bear a heavy load. The verse says:
A sheep wrapped in tiger skin still reveals its spots; though its essential nature is pitiable, it remains but frail.
Having found satisfaction on the grass before the slope for a mere morning, one suddenly perceives the drifting clouds parting and returning again.
Lingyuan said: "The elders of recent times involve themselves in two kinds of conditions; their wisdom and understanding are not clear, and they lose the true body of the Dharma. One...
One should encounter adverse conditions; thus one frequently encounters the wind of decline. One should encounter favorable conditions; thus one frequently encounters the wind of profit.

Once touched by these two winds, the vapors of joy and anger intersect within the heart, and repressed, turbulent expressions float upon the face. This leads to bringing disgrace upon the Dharma-gate and subjecting the worthy and enlightened to ridicule.
The commentary says: Seeking profit because of decline, and encountering decline while craving profit—if there were not such a wind blowing, [this would not occur].
To act thus can truly be called the mark of a worthy and enlightened person. The verse says:
A single-leafed skiff floats upon the vast and boundless; Observing the favorability or opposition of the winds, one steers the mast and sails.
If one is certain to skillfully maneuver the tiller, One shall ferry beings across Jambudvīpa to the Land of Bliss.

Yuánwù Qín said: "Who among men is without fault? To be able to reform one's faults after they have occurred—no goodness is greater than this. Only the wise are able to reform their faults and shift toward the good, whereas the foolish mostly conceal their faults and gloss over their errors.

He added: "To reform one’s faults without regret transforms folly into wisdom; yet, alas, what can be done about those who do not recognize their own faults? He then offered this verse: Who among men is without fault? To reform them after they occur is the greatest good. Only the wise can reform and shift toward virtue; The foolish mostly conceal faults and gloss over errors.
Reforming faults without regret turns folly into wisdom— But what can be done for those who do not recognize their own faults?
Holding biased views and refusing to reform one's goodness; acting with barbaric arrogance and relying on strength, one daily incurs transgressions.
To start anew and cast off old habits—when what is crooked is made straight and what is curved is made whole.
Yuanwu said to Miaoxi: "In all human conduct, one should be as careful at the end as at the beginning, so that no failure occurs. Long ago...

Old Master Huìtáng said: "The Venerable Hóngshèng of Huangbò was also an extraordinary patch-robed monk; it was only in his later years that he went astray. Looking at his beginning, one cannot but call him worthy. He added:

"To remain as one from beginning to end must belong to a family of great prudence. He further remarked: "As for his final move, no one has yet been able to fathom its meaning. He then offered this verse: Huangbò’s staff strikes the ground three times, Then he says, "Do you understand? If you say you understand, you are a blind man; If you say you do not understand, you are deaf. The old fellow’s words are like a thunderclap;
How could they ever be grasped by the intellect? If you wish to see the true face of Huangbò, Look directly at the staff in your hand.
"At first one should exert effort, later one may follow the natural course; When decline reaches the point of contradiction, it provokes weariness and resentment.
Reflecting on the errors of late life in ancient times, One should broaden learning while summarizing ritual to protect oneself throughout one's entire life.
Fojian Qin said to Fodeng Xun: "A person of lofty character does not take fame or rank as a source of honor; they have mastered the underlying principle."

Such a person is not distressed by suppression or frustration. Those who receive favor and exert their strength, or see profit and offer their sincerity, all act as those of middling or inferior capacity.
The commentary says: This reveals the excellence of the superior man and exposes the shortcomings of the base and inferior.
The Buddha-mirror regards a single word as wisdom. The verse says:
"Honor and disgrace cannot shift the will of the gentleman; With eyes empty of the world, he plays at ease.
Knowing gratitude and repaying virtue, he accepts the iron collar; In the end, he belongs to those who follow and serve, obeying his commands."
Fojian said: "Master Baoyun once told Attendant Ning, 'To maintain the Way and remain content in poverty is the natural lot of a patch-robed monk.

One whose maintenance of the Way is shifted by success or failure, by fortune or misfortune, cannot yet be said to speak of the Way. [The Master] comments: How profound are these words on maintaining the Way;
they serve as a warning for those who would alter their integrity. The verse says:"
Since ancient times, it has been said that while the body may be poor, the Way is not poor. Wearing straw sandals and carrying a bamboo staff, one sheds the dust of the mundane world.
Were it not for constant self-discipline and steadfast integrity, who could remain sincere when emotions arise in pursuit of external circumstances?

As Master Fojian said: "If one does not worry about the Way, then one's cultivation of the mind will not be distant; if one always keeps the body at ease, then the application of one's will will not be distracted."
Great! The ancients underwent hardships and experienced perils before they could enjoy lifelong peace. [The Master] picks up the theme, saying:
"If one harbors even a single thought of enjoying such peace, let alone 'greatness'—one might as well stop speaking. The verse says:
His resolve was honed through hardships, making it steadfast; his path was pursued with diligent toil and focused intent.
Thus he earned the reputation of being most excellent, possessing white eyebrows, inspiring in others a longing and yearning for such a fortunate encounter.
Master Fuyan said: "The demeanor when presiding over the assembly must be solemn even on days of leisure; the speech when addressing guests should [be appropriate]..."
He was solemn even during moments of private intimacy. He remarked, "To be refined and cautious in one's private leisure is precisely the strategy for withdrawing from the world to avoid harm.
He further said, "If what one says is necessarily as what one does, how can there be any question of partiality or bias? He then offered this verse:
Zhengse was especially able to exercise caution with his speech; amidst the great court and vast assemblies, he maintained a solemn and dignified bearing.
Furthermore, in matters of entering the chamber and seizing the opportune moment, he was rigorous and reverent, establishing the Dharma-gate.
Foyan said: "A student must not become mired in words and language. For words and language are dependent upon others."
To form an intellectual understanding obstructs the gate of self-awakening; one cannot transcend the realm of words and images. He remarked:
"If one has attained awakening yet relies on intellectual understanding as a livelihood, does this not obstruct the gate of birth and death? Reflect upon this. The verse says:
The reason for the name is that it has from the beginning obstructed pure vision; once swept clean, the fundamental light of knowledge manifests.
It is said that its tranquil illumination pervades as many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges, yet the faculty of the nose remains as before, floating above the face.
Master Gaoyuan said: "If human emotions are not restrained, they run wild and cause disorder. Therefore, one must eliminate emotion, cease delusion, and prohibit evil."

Cease this heterodoxy. One cannot, for a single moment, abandon the compass and square. The Master picks up the phrase and says: "If one uses the compass and square to regulate others, yet allows one's own deluded emotions to become disordered and chaotic—is that possible? He then offers a verse:
When delusion is exhausted and passions dissolved, awakening is wondrously luminous; With every action and every step, one accords with original perfection.
Relying on these rules, the governance of the realm flourishes; People delight in their vocations, families live in peace, and we celebrate great tranquility.

Gao’an Wu said: "When I first traveled to the Patriarchal Mountains, I saw Master Fojian’s small-scale sermon (xiaocan), which stated that greed, desire, anger, and hatred—[are the root of suffering]."

Like an enemy thief, one should oppose them with wisdom. Although he was young at the time, [the Master] knew in his heart that he was a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend), and so he requested to be admitted as a resident monk.
[The Master] remarked: "If one possesses wisdom, one may indeed act as a virtuous friend; yet what can be done about the thieves of greed and anger, which cannot be driven out?
He then spoke this verse:
"Penetrate until love and hate are extinguished; Use the mind to cast them out until the essence is revealed.
How is it when in stillness? *Svāhā*! Firmly plant your heels as if cast from cast iron. Gao’an said:
"The persistence of the student must be centered and upright; though they may suffer a hundred setbacks, they remain grand and free of anxiety. Or perhaps..."

Their inclinations are biased and depraved; morning and night they are preoccupied with schemes for profit and gain. I fear that such magnificent bodies will find no place between heaven and earth. [The Master] remarked:
"To strive for profit until one has nowhere to set foot is ultimately not as good as maintaining rectitude without seeking anything—thus to be vast and unconfined within heaven and earth.
The verse says: Morning and night, they scheme for gain; They have nowhere to set their feet. Better to preserve integrity and seek nothing at all, So as to be vast and free within heaven and earth.
Azure cypresses withstand the freezing cold, standing firm without withering; Supporting the heavens, their upright form is uniquely distinguished.
Wildflowers by the stream do not suffer the bitterness of wind and frost; They bloom brilliantly before the dawn and fade after it. Gao’an said:
"Virtue, Way, Benevolence, and Righteousness are not possessed solely by those of antiquity; they are also present in people of today. Because...
Delusory thoughts and emotional attachments have accumulated through long habituation until they are thick and heavy; one cannot eliminate them all at once.
This is why one fails to reach the state of the ancients. [The Master] comments: Why not cultivate and maintain yourself by taking those who possess virtue and benevolence as your model?
Why do you instead merely indulge in self-indulgence and self-abandonment? The verse says:
Comparing the past with the present, the difference is vast; the true mind is pursued by delusion as false thoughts blaze.
If one is willing to gradually eliminate habitual tendencies, one will surely extend the Way and its righteousness alongside the sages of old.
Gao’an retired from Yunju. When Yuanwu wished to restore Wolong Hermitage as a place for his retirement, the hermitage master said, "Among those beneath the forest..."
If a person truly possesses the joy of the Way and righteousness, the physical form may be cast aside. Furthermore, the Western Mountains and Mount Lu have forests and springs that lie side by side;
these are all places where I may dwell in leisure in my old age. Why must one possess such things for oneself before one can find joy?
[The Master] remarked: "This is an act free from entanglement. Yet those who plan to build mountain hermitages and boast of their pleasure—upon hearing this, could they not feel ashamed?"
Is it within the mind? A verse says:
"The spirit transcends the realm of forms, severed from all entanglements; At ease among mountains and forests, the weary old man rests in leisure.
Do not mock those who labor for private possessions; When rooms are spread out and houses are dilapidated, whom can they ask to repair them?"
Guīyún originally said: "Nothing has more severely weakened moral instruction than the sycophant; even upright men and true scholars are skillfully led into their influence.
[The Master] remarked: "I ask you, who is it that can discern the sycophant? He then spoke this verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
Deceitful and perverse, they exclusively practice evil desires; they subvert the fundamental principles and corrupt the regulations, swaying one another back and forth.
Were it not for those whose discernment and verification are utterly refined and precise, they would be tainted by the poison of delusion and wait for their own destruction.
Yuanji Cen said: "The Buddha’s era is far distant, and the True Dharma has grown faint. The exemplary standards of the monastic groves are nearly swept away from the ground."

"Even if there were someone to support and rescue him, [the Emperor] instead treated him as a 'barbarian king. The Master remarked, "I say that supporting and rescuing is precisely the compassion of a Bodhisattva.
He then offered this verse:
A great man who upholds the right way and weaves the threads of dharma; One who sacrifices his body to restore the ancient pivot of the Way.
If you do not follow this principle of honoring and establishing a model for teachers, You will merely listen to arbitrary assignments and become a lowly slave.
Dongshan spoke in vain of acting as an elder and residing in the abbot’s quarters; He was simply the same Empty Seat (Kōjōza) from before, letting conditions take their course.
Dwelling. Without making plans for tomorrow. He remarks: "The words of 'relying on conditions' are sworn upon one's seat. The verse says:
With gourd ladle and staff, the abbot dwells surrounded by wandering clouds and waters; When shall we compare the extent of our karmic conditions?
The original face is as it was in the past, so it is now; Everywhere in the fragrant spring, birds sing from the trees.
Zhe-weng Yan said: "Those who currently occupy the abbot’s quarters do not merely scrape away the contents of others' alms bowls to indulge their own appetites;
they also cultivate favors with the hope of being transferred to a great monastery. I fear that one day Old Iron-Face Yan (Yama) will settle the accounts.
He remarked: 'Upon hearing this account of those who use bribery to transfer to a major monastery, how could one not be struck with alarm?'"
The verse says:
To misappropriate monastic property and use it unrighteously— With a deceitful heart, one falls into the Iron Ring Mountains.
Though you may boast of power as heavy as Mount Tai, The karmic mirror is held high, and your confession will be fully exposed.

Xuetang Xing said: "In studying the Way, one remains serene regarding external things and has no preferences or cravings. To the point of forgetting rank and position, and discarding fame and beauty, it seems as though these are accomplished without effort. He added: "For one who is without desire, sounds and status are truly not objects of inclination. Why? Because a square block does not fit into a round hole. The verse says: The square block does not fit the round hole; The Way is not sought through external things. When the mind is free from craving, It naturally transcends all worldly concerns. If you wish to attain the Way, Do not look for it outside yourself. If you seek it elsewhere, You will never find it. If you can let go of all attachments, This is called the true practice of the Way. Do not be deluded by appearances; Seek the Way within your own nature. If you can see your own nature, You will realize the ultimate truth. This is what is meant by "the Way. Do not seek it in books or teachings; Seek it in your own heart. If you can see your own heart, You will understand the source of all phenomena. This is what is meant by "understanding the source. Do not be bound by forms or names; Be free from all conceptualizations. If you can be free from conceptualization, This is called liberation. Liberation is not found in emptiness; It is found in the midst of activity. Activity is not separate from stillness; Stillness is not separate from activity. Activity and stillness are one; This is called the Great Way. The Great Way is vast and boundless; It cannot be grasped or described. Only those with great wisdom Can enter this gate. If you can enter this gate, You will see the Buddha-nature. The Buddha-nature is not far away; It is right here before you. If you can recognize it, You will attain the fruit of Buddhahood. This is what is meant by "attaining the fruit. Do not be deluded by words and phrases; Words are merely pointers. If you rely on the pointing finger, You will miss the moon. If you can put down the finger, You will see the moon. Seeing the moon is seeing the Way; This is the ultimate truth. Do not doubt this teaching; Practice it with diligence. If you practice with diligence, You will surely attain enlightenment. This is the instruction of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Do not fail to take it to heart. Take it to heart and practice it; Then you will realize the Way. This is the final word. Do not seek it elsewhere. Seek it within yourself. If you can find it within yourself, You have attained the Way. Attaining the Way is not difficult; It is simply a matter of letting go. Letting go of all attachments, This is the essence of the Way. The essence of the Way is empty and tranquil; It is beyond thought and description. Beyond thought and description, This is the true nature of reality. The true nature of reality is the Buddha; The Buddha is our own original face. Our original face is always present; We just do not recognize it. If we can recognize it, We are already Buddhas. Being a Buddha is not a matter of greatness; It is simply being as one is. Being as one is is the Way; The Way is not something to be sought. Seeking is itself a delusion; Delusion is the root of suffering. To cut off delusion, One must see the nature. Seeing the nature is seeing the Buddha; This is the ultimate goal. Do not be distracted by external things; Focus on your own mind. If you focus on your own mind, You will see the Way clearly. Seeing the Way clearly, You will transcend birth and death. Transcending birth and death, You will attain eternal peace. Eternal peace is Nirvana; Nirvana is the ultimate bliss. This is the teaching of the Buddhas. Do not doubt it; Practice it with faith. With faith and practice, You will surely attain the Way. This is the final instruction. Take it to heart and act upon it. Act upon it and you will be liberated. Liberation is the fruit of the Way. May all beings attain this fruit. Amen.

When worldly thoughts cease, the thought of the Way prevails; the physical body stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, while honor, splendor, wealth, and nobility are but floating clouds. At the silent gate of Chan, one must always press forward.
Sijin Xin said: "Frugality and letting go are the most direct paths for entering the Way. [The Master] added: "If you let go, then the Way..."
It manifests before you of its own accord; even the single character "enter" is unnecessary. The verse says:
One who simplifies affairs is truly a person who accomplishes them; Their dignified conduct is upright and pure.
Needless to speak of reaching Chang’an beyond the city walls— They trample through the river plum blossoms, rejoicing in early spring.
Sishin said to Zhantang: "Among students, those who possess talent and discernment, as well as loyalty, trustworthiness, integrity, and righteousness, are the highest type.

Those whose talent may not be great but who are prudent and possess a sense of measure are the next. As for those who harbor deviance and wait for opportunities, changing their ways according to circumstances—they are the lowest."

"This is truly a petty person. [The Master] adds: "In discerning the character of men, we must acknowledge Sīsin; yet, alas, how can one help it that those who are loyal and prudent are few, while petty people abound? The verse says:
The eminent and worthy strike their foreheads, hoping for one who appears but once in an age; they lament the prevalence of the treacherous and the false, shedding tears in profusion.
Even if compassionate instruction were used to refine and mold them well, the habits formed into custom will ultimately remain impossible to restrain.
Qing of the Hermitage Hall said: "The requirements of a *zhuchi* (abbot) lie in being cautious and reverent regarding the faults of partiality and unilateral authority. He then added: "I dare ask—"
Question: Can those who occupy positions of authority avoid these two defects? The verse says:

Slanderous words easily enter the ear and cause estrangement and hatred; Opposing the hearts of the multitude while relying on one's own abilities leads to isolation and peril, with no one to replace one. One must endure the hardships of braving both cold and heat.
Cao Tang said: "The abbot must examine human nature and have a thorough knowledge of those above and below. He added:
"The wise can observe and understand this; the foolish do the opposite. The verse says:
He examined the circumstances of the assembly to determine their suitability, and analyzed their spiritual capacities to distinguish between superior and inferior.
Adopting these skillful means to guide them accordingly, he dared to ensure that heaven would endure long and earth remain firm.
At Mount Shantang, he first declined the summons from Caoshan; when the Prefect sent an official letter urging him to accept, his reply stated: "If one were to..."

"Eating fine rice and chewing fatty meats to become a 'patch-robed monk' (śramaṇa) who craves fame is not as good as wearing grass clothes and eating wood for sustenance to be a wild man of Mount Yin.
[The Master] comments: "The censure of craving fame strikes directly at the malady of patch-robed monks in the present age;
yet, those who subsist on wood for the rest of their lives likely do not exist either. He offers this verse:

When seeing profit, think only of righteousness; thus one may follow the Way with ease. Leisurely beyond the realm of things, far surpassing the common herd, one places oneself among hills and valleys, yet this is not mere desolation.
The Way resides in the deep crags, permitting intimacy with the distant kin.
Shantang said: "Matters of the world must not be pursued to their extreme. To pursue them to the extreme leads to calamity and chaos. [The Master] added: "To pursue them to the extreme..."
These matters are all the deeds of those who have no sense of shame. The verse says:
When power is exhausted and strength spent, anxiety and suffering arise; Rest content with your lot and govern yourself—cease striving for achievement.
Leave behind what remains and do not exhaust your feelings; On the Double Ninth Festival, the chrysanthemums are still seen in full bloom.

Miaoxi Gaoyun said: "Liking and disliking, difference and sameness—these are the common sentiments of humanity; only the wise and the enlightened are not turned by them. He then picked up the theme, saying:
"If one is truly clear and penetrating, one can still turn others. He then offered this verse:
Consciousness is vast and its measure wide; observe the inner sincerity of the multitude. Allow them to intermingle as they may, yet judge from within.
Knowing early on that the ocean of nature surges with waves, hold fast to the rudder’s tip and the path of the ship will open.
Miaoxi said: "When various quarters nominate an Elder, one must nominate those who maintain the Way and withdraw in tranquility; thus their will and integrity shall remain firm."
Wherever he went, he established monastic communities (*saṅghārāma*). As the master of the Dharma, he sought to remedy the corruptions of the present day.
Yet there are those who are cunning and sycophantic, who know no shame and flatter themselves into positions of power, forming alliances with the gates of the influential and noble.

Why then need they be mentioned? The Master says: "To 'recommend' (*jǔ*) means to select; it certainly does not imply partiality or favoritism. That one accepts such alliances is clear enough. Nevertheless, there are those who resemble the Way."
"But as for those who are actually treacherous—if you raise them up, what then? The verse says:
"To remedy a failing, one must possess the correct eye; To merely recommend those who withdraw in tranquility is also to carry a heavy burden.
Though one's sincere heart is revealed piece by piece, those who understand it are rare; It causes Bian He to grieve, his jade hidden within his breast."
Yinshouzuo said to Wan’an, “One who calls himself a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) should wash his mind until it is upright and impartial, so as to receive those coming from the four quarters.

Washing away the mind’s depravity by mountain slopes and water’s edge, Its radiance responding to things is most praiseworthy.
How can it compare to those who "wear three" or "don five," Making their monastic gates as noisy and chaotic as a marketplace?
The Head Seat said: "Which abbot does not wish to establish a forest monastery? Yet few are able to revitalize one. This is because..."

They forget the Way and its Virtue; they abandon benevolence and righteousness; they discard laws and measures; and it is by indulging private sentiments that such things come to pass. [The Master] remarks:

A forest of wolves and jackals, a gathering of beasts; they call out to their kind and rely on one another for support.
They seek only to lead others astray for the sake of fame, leaving the high and low paths of the Patriarchs utterly muddled.

Regarding Master Yan of Wan’an’s practice of frugality, he used his small formal discourses (*xiao can*) and general lectures (*pu shuo*) as offerings. Among the monks, there were some who privately criticized this.
The Master said, "To enjoy rich delicacies in the morning and grow weary of coarse grain in the evening is the common sentiment of man.

Since you all consider the matter of birth and death to be great, and have sought me out on these desolate shores, you should reflect that your spiritual practice is not yet complete and that the time since the Sage departed is remote;
how can you occupy yourselves with gluttony morning and night? He added, "Since it concerns birth and death, even a single meal should be regarded [with mindfulness]."
Those who shamelessly propose frugality are all nothing but gluttonous types. The verse says:
"Simple, solid, and extraordinary— A brilliant diamond bursting forth from a cold forge.
Why begrudge its worth of hundreds of thousands? What need is there to compete with the chaff and husks at the mill?"
Dian Shouzuo said to Hunrong, "If a patch-robed monk lacks inner virtue yet relies outwardly on flowery rhetoric and cleverness, it is like a leaking ship heavily painted with vermilion and cinnabar;
though a puppet might look impressive as it is driven across dry land, once it ventures onto rivers and lakes and encounters wind and waves, will it not be in peril?
[The Master] added: "Patch-robed monks are weary and dejected, fearing the wind and waves for their entire lives."
No achievement has been accomplished; thus, it may be set aside as a mere model. The verse says:
"Playing with cleverness, the sprout frolics— What does this have to do with the great task of governance, pacifying chaos and restoring order?
A master of the Way is broken; Rowing a boat across the Milky Way while walking on level ground."
Fozhi says: "That the wandering consciousness does not dare to seize upon objects is due to the power of awakening-illumination. He adds:

Racing through the karmic consciousness arises from delusion; wherever it is blown by the winds of sensory objects, it settles there.
If you are willing to turn back and personally examine this, you will mount a wooden horse and ascend a golden ladder.

Content with poverty and delighting in the Way, he leans against the edge of a cliff;
Accustomed to digging into the void and roasting it in the earth until every trace of conceptual thought is exhausted. Do not disdain the patchwork robe accumulating dust and ash. Zhu’an Guang said:
"To lead oneself and face the assembly, one must rely on wisdom; to dispel delusion and eliminate emotion, one must first attain awakening. [The Master] added: "I pick this up [to say]:..."

Regulations and expedient means all accord with the proper measure; Upholding impartiality, the clear mirror is without distinction.
A teacher such as this presides over the dense forest; Like the autumn moon, its pure radiance is bright and clean.
Zhu’an said: "Those of superficial learning and shallow reception merely value what they hear while despising what they see; in the end, none can fathom its profound mysteries. He added:

"If one transmits orally and receives by ear without possessing the true eye, there is no difference from the class of those who merely parrot words. He then offered this verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions]

Gathering scraps from the edges of one’s lips, Stuffing them into the field of the chest to form a womb of calamity— A lifetime spent entirely in blindness and delusion, Stumbling blindly into a heap of skulls. Miyun Yuanjie said:
"There are three things a monastic must avoid: Do not fear when affairs are many; Do not seek out when there is nothing to do; Do not engage in disputes over right and wrong."
Discrimination. If the abbot understands these three points, he will not be deluded by external things. [The Master] comments: "Carefully guard the family gate;
let every matter rest in the mind. What is meant by "do not"? Is it not to simplify affairs and attend to one's own fundamental nature? It is further said:
To reproach others is not as good as reproaching oneself. The verse says:
When presiding over the assembly, one should cleanse one’s thoughts; Relinquishing everything with the body, practice only broad forbearance.
Gazing calmly at the blue dogs and white clouds arise— How is this any different from willow catkins flying over a spring embankment?

Mimian said: "If a patch-robed monk’s conduct is crooked and depraved, and he has long possessed traces of unwholesome behavior that are known throughout the monastic community, this is not worth resenting.
However, when the multitude deems someone virtuous while he is in reality unworthy, this is truly something to be resented. [The Master] adds:
"To appear virtuous while being actually unworthy is precisely how those who are perverse and sycophantic are able to delude the masses. He further says:
If one regards the unworthy as virtuous, who could be more pitiable? The verse says:
To gnash teeth at power-hungry villains leaves a deep legacy of sorrow; To expose their treachery and recklessness serves as a warning.
I urge the assembly across the seas to take heed and be alert: When eating rice, one bites into grit—whose pain can be forbidden?
Zide Hui said: "A patch-robed monk who is sincere and oriented toward the correct, though foolish, may still be of use;
one who is sycophantic and harbors evil, though wise, will ultimately cause harm. He added: "To abandon wisdom and draw near to folly is not merely to avoid harm;
it is truly an exhortation to cultivate sincerity and correctness. The verse says:
"Be reverent and diligent, always acting according to the rules; do not be frivolous. Relying on the light to seek the heavy, you shall never fail.
As for abandoning righteousness to serve the sycophantic and the crafty—this is like the cat that fails to complete its painting and ends up resembling a dog.
Prime Minister Qian Xiangxian requested that Huo’an take charge of the Tiansheng Monastery to manifest his transcendence of the world. Huo’an said, "I will not..."

"Unhooking the head of a hanging sheep to sell dog meat"—he then fled under the cover of night. [The Master] remarked: "Setting aside for a moment the fact that he was not such a master of his craft, was he truly 'the one beneath the forest'? He then offered this verse: Unhooking the sheep’s head to sell dog meat, He vanished into the night.
Setting aside the question of whether he was a true adept, Was he truly the one beneath the forest?
Idle and indolent, I am weary of universal socializing; Perched haughtily on a solitary peak, I avoid the pursuit of fame.
Yet as soon as I follow the crowd, my true form is exposed; It is difficult to evade when karmic conditions entangle one’s feet.

Words and phrases appear together with tracks and footprints; Chattering on and on, one only wins a ruined monastery.

Xiatang Yuan said: "A student of the Way must first rectify their mind; only then can they rectify themselves and others."

Regarding the word "Object" (*wu*): He held it up and said, "I dare ask: how is the mind made correct? Is it being correct if one does not harbor private interests and does not pursue external objects?
What connection is there [between that and correctness]? He then offered this verse:
All things are without mind, yet the mind itself is numinous; It revolves through ten thousand transformations and all affairs are accomplished.
Exhaustively described as the divine function, it is skillfully round and turning;

Its original clarity is as pure as ice and frost. Compassionately receiving this profound meaning, Jingshan Nan said: "In recent years, the Chan school has become desolate; in various quarters, the smoke has dispersed and the assemblies have scattered."

"Only our elder brother remained unmoved in spirit. Were it not for one whose Way is full and virtue is substantial, whose practice and understanding correspond with one another, how could such a person be found so often?

"Living uprightly in his place, he did not join the vulgar stream; He was resentful toward the petty crowd who created offenses and faults.

If even a hair’s breadth of emotional views remains unexhausted, this is the very root of birth and death. [The Master] comments: If one awakens to the Way yet does not resolve birth and death, it is entirely due to emotional views.
As for those who exhaust emotional views yet still face birth and death—please let a true spiritual friend decide this matter. Verse:

"Awakened awareness is liberated, neither arising nor ceasing; Furthermore, wandering thoughts are dissolved and obstructed, and the circular light behind the head is as brilliant as a mirror. *Buddhāya*—this is their array."
